The standard architectural fixes are ReLU activations (whose derivative is 1 for positive inputs, not <1) and residual/skip connections (which add a gradient highway that bypasses the multiplication chain).

misconception_identified: Learner conflates positional encoding with a sequence compression operation. Positional encoding adds position information to individual token embeddings; it does not compress the full sequence into a fixed-length context vector. That description maps to the encoder bottleneck in pre-Transformer seq2seq models — the very bottleneck Transformers were designed to eliminate.
evaluator_notes: Answer B was selected, which incorrectly attributes the bottleneck elimination to positional encoding performing sequence compression. This is a fundamental misconception about what positional encoding does. The correct answer (C) describes the QKᵀ pairwise score matrix that gives every token O(1) direct access to every other token. No explanation was provided to assess reasoning.
feedback_for_learner: Positional encoding only injects position signals into each token's embedding — it does not compress or summarize the sequence. The actual bottleneck elimination comes from the attention matrix: QKᵀ produces an N×N grid where every pair of positions interacts directly in one matrix operation, so token 1 and token 500 are exactly one step apart regardless of sequence length. The RNN bottleneck arises because information must flow through 499 sequential state transitions; attention collapses that path length to O(1).

evaluator_notes: Learner correctly identifies the motivation for idempotency (non-atomic async multi-step loops), lists valid failure scenarios (double transactions, broken state, unnecessary reprocessing, race conditions), and connects it to resumability and debuggability. However, the formal property definition — the core of what the question asked — is never stated: a step is idempotent if executing it multiple times produces the same result as executing it once (f(f(x)) = f(x)). Without this, the answer explains why idempotency matters but not what it is. The question explicitly asked for this property.
feedback_for_learner: Good coverage of failure modes and motivations. The missing piece is the formal definition: a step is idempotent if applying it N times yields the same outcome as applying it once. Concretely: a database write using INSERT OR REPLACE (upsert) is idempotent — running it twice leaves one record. A plain INSERT is not — running it twice creates a duplicate. In agentic loops, designing every step to be an upsert/overwrite rather than an append means any crashed step can be safely retried without auditing prior state.
